title: How Long Will $2 Million Last in Retirement? Exact Years
metaDescription: How long will $2 million last in retirement? See exact years by monthly spending and real return, what the return alone pays, and the 30-year ceiling.
h1: How Long Will $2 Million Last in Retirement?
cardBlurb: Modeled years a $2,000,000 balance lasts at six monthly spending levels and four real returns, plus what living on the return alone pays.
introText:
A $2,000,000 nest egg lasts anywhere from about 10 years to more than 45 years depending on your monthly spending and real portfolio return. At a flat withdrawal of $8,000 a month in today's dollars, your balance lasts about 20.8 years with a 0% real return, 27 years at a 2% real return, and 44.9 years at a 4% real return. If your investments generate a 4% real return each year, the return covers $6,666.67 a month without reducing your starting principal balance at all.

Modeling in real dollars means your withdrawals rise alongside inflation each year to maintain the exact same standard of living throughout your post-career life.

sections.heading: How Long $2,000,000 Lasts at Different Monthly Spending Levels
sections.body:
Your monthly spending level determines whether a $2,000,000 portfolio lasts about 10 years or more than 45 years. In our internal modeling, we ran $2,000,000 through the same engine as our [withdrawal calculator](/investing/withdrawal-calculator/) at four real returns and six monthly spending levels to see how many years each lasts. Using flat withdrawals in today's dollars taken at the end of each month, the balance earns an annual return compounded monthly at the annual rate divided by 12. Because all inputs and outputs are documented here, you can verify each scenario using our calculators.

| Monthly Spending | 0% Real Return | 2% Real Return | 4% Real Return | 5% Real Return |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $6,000 | 27.8 years | 40.6 years | Does not run out | Does not run out |
| $6,666.67 | 25.0 years | 34.8 years | Does not run out | Does not run out |
| $8,000 | 20.8 years | 27.0 years | 44.9 years | Does not run out |
| $10,000 | 16.7 years | 20.3 years | 27.6 years | 35.9 years |
| $12,000 | 13.9 years | 16.3 years | 20.3 years | 23.8 years |
| $16,000 | 10.4 years | 11.8 years | 13.5 years | 14.8 years |

A real return represents your portfolio growth after subtracting the rate of inflation. For instance, if an investment portfolio produces a 7% nominal gain while consumer prices rise by 3%, the real return comes out to approximately 3.9% via the formula (1.07 / 1.03) - 1. Holding withdrawals flat in real dollars means the physical check you write to yourself increases each year with inflation to match your baseline expenses.

The break-even point occurs when monthly withdrawals equal the monthly growth generated by your balance. When you pull out $6,666.67 a month at a 4% real return, your portfolio generates $80,000 per year in real growth. That earnings rate matches your $80,000 annual draw dollar for dollar. Under those baseline conditions, the money does not run out in the mathematical model because the principal never gets touched.

sections.heading: Can You Live on the Interest Alone
sections.body:
You can live off the interest and real returns of a $2,000,000 balance if your annual household budget remains at or below your portfolio yield. When you restrict distributions to the real gains produced each month, the starting $2,000,000 principal remains intact indefinitely.

- 2% real return: $40,000 a year, which provides $3,333.33 a month.
- 3% real return: $60,000 a year, which provides $5,000.00 a month.
- 4% real return: $80,000 a year, which provides $6,666.67 a month.
- 5% real return: $100,000 a year, which provides $8,333.33 a month.

The historical origin of the 4% rule connects directly to research published by Cooley, Hubbard, and Walz in the [AAII Journal Trinity Study](https://www.aaii.com/journal/article/retirement-savings-choosing-a-withdrawal-rate-that-is-sustainable). That study evaluated historical market periods and reported that an initial withdrawal of about 4% of the starting balance in year one, adjusted upward for inflation in each subsequent year, lasted 30 years across most historical periods for portfolios holding a large share of stocks. For a $2,000,000 account, a 4% initial withdrawal translates to $80,000 in the first year, or $6,666.67 a month.

This interest-only strategy is not for households needing more than $6,666.67 a month or whose portfolios yield 2% or 3% in real terms. Retirees needing higher monthly cash flow must plan to spend down their principal rather than attempting to preserve the entire $2,000,000 balance.

sections.heading: How Much You Can Spend for 20, 25, 30 and 35 Years
sections.body:
Retirees planning for a specific timeline can calculate the maximum sustainable monthly draw that exhausts the balance at the end of their target horizon. Life expectancy arithmetic dictates your required planning window. If you retire at age 65 and plan to age 90, you need 25 years of cash flow. Retiring at age 60 requires 30 years of coverage, while retiring early at age 55 demands 35 full years.

The table below outlines the highest flat monthly withdrawal in today's dollars that uses up a $2,000,000 balance across fixed retirement windows:

| Retirement Horizon | 0% Real Return | 2% Real Return | 4% Real Return | 5% Real Return |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 20 Years | $8,333.33 / month | $10,117.67 / month | $12,119.61 / month | $13,199.11 / month |
| 25 Years | $6,666.67 / month | $8,477.09 / month | $10,556.74 / month | $11,691.80 / month |
| 30 Years | $5,555.56 / month | $7,392.39 / month | $9,548.31 / month | $10,736.43 / month |
| 35 Years | $4,761.90 / month | $6,625.26 / month | $8,855.49 / month | $10,093.75 / month |

For a standard 30-year horizon, the highest flat monthly withdrawal spans from $5,555.56 with zero real growth to $9,548.31 at a 4% real return. Lengthening your timeline to 35 years reduces the sustainable 4% monthly draw down to $8,855.49. To test dynamic options where you alter distributions based on market performance, review our guide on [retirement withdrawal strategies](/guides/retirement-withdrawal-strategies/).

sections.heading: What Changes the Years
sections.body:
Mathematical projections rely on steady annual returns and fixed spending, but several practical factors alter how long 2 million dollars will last in retirement. Understanding these friction points helps you prevent premature portfolio depletion.

First, taxes reduce your net spendable income. Distributions from traditional 401(k) and traditional IRA accounts are subject to ordinary income taxes, meaning a $10,000 gross monthly withdrawal does not equal $10,000 of grocery and housing money. You can map out your total after-tax receipts across accounts with our [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/).

Second, spending rarely stays perfectly flat in real terms. While holding withdrawals flat in today's dollars accounts for average consumer inflation, specific budget categories like medical care and long-term assistance often accelerate faster. A sudden spike in late-life assisted living expenses can shorten an otherwise stable 30-year runway.

Third, sequence-of-returns risk can disrupt steady averages. A severe market downturn early in retirement can exhaust a $2,000,000 portfolio years earlier than a steady average return calculation indicates.

Fourth, guaranteed income streams lengthen your timeline by reducing how much you need to withdraw from your nest egg. Outside Social Security and other income payments absorb baseline overhead. If you receive monthly Social Security, your required portfolio draw drops, extending how long your portfolio lasts. You can estimate your government benefit schedule using our [Social Security retirement calculator](/retirement/social-security-retirement-calculator/).

Fifth, for couples, our model evaluates overall household spending rather than individual living expenses. Two individuals sharing a single $2,000,000 pool must budget their combined lifestyle under one total monthly distribution. If you want to compare how different wealth tiers perform under similar rules, see our guides on [how long 150k lasts in retirement](/guides/how-long-will-150k-last-in-retirement/), [how long 1 million will last in retirement](/guides/how-long-will-1-million-last-in-retirement/), or whether [3 million is enough to retire at 40](/guides/is-3-million-enough-to-retire-at-40/).

Our projections would change if your portfolio experiences sustained negative real returns, if you carry unhedged long-term health liabilities, or if tax rates on your retirement plan distributions rise significantly.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
Based on our internal modeling, a $2,000,000 balance lasts across typical retirement horizons when spending stays aligned with real growth. For a 30-year retirement, $2,000,000 supports a flat monthly draw in today's dollars of about $5,560 with no portfolio growth, about $7,390 at a 2% real return, and about $9,550 at a 4% real return.

Living on the return alone requires your ongoing real return to match or exceed your withdrawal rate. At a 4% real return, your annual earnings cover $6,666.67 a month while leaving the full starting balance untouched. At a 2% real return, that interest-only income drops to $3,333.33 a month.

This $2,000,000 milestone fits a retiree whose planned household spending sits below these thresholds. Your personal runway will lengthen or contract based on investment taxes, unexpected healthcare obligations, and market sequences in your initial retirement years. To establish your target, calculate your baseline living expenses, identify your outside guaranteed income, and size your monthly withdrawal using our interactive tools.

faqs.question: What does a $2 million retirement look like?
faqs.answer: A $2,000,000 retirement supports monthly spending between $6,000 and $16,000 in today's dollars depending on your timeline and return. At $8,000 a month, the balance lasts 20.8 years at 0% real return, 27 years at 2%, and 44.9 years at 4%. At $10,000 a month, it lasts 16.7 years at 0%, 20.3 years at 2%, and 27.6 years at 4%.

faqs.question: Can I live off the interest on $2 million?
faqs.answer: You can live off the interest if your spending matches real portfolio gains. A 2% real return provides $3,333.33 a month, a 3% real return yields $5,000 a month, a 4% real return pays $6,666.67 a month, and a 5% real return generates $8,333.33 a month while keeping the starting principal balance completely intact.

faqs.question: How many years will $1 million last in retirement?
faqs.answer: The results for $2,000,000 are not simply double the years of $1,000,000, the same years need double the spending, so see our guide on [how long 1 million will last in retirement](/guides/how-long-will-1-million-last-in-retirement/) for exact schedules.

faqs.question: How long will $2 million last for a couple?
faqs.answer: The model tracks total household spending rather than marital status, so $2,000,000 lasts as long as a couple's combined spending allows. For example, if a couple spends a combined $8,000 a month in today's dollars, their money will last 20.8 years with zero growth, 27 years at a 2% real return, and 44.9 years at 4%.

faqs.question: How long will $2 million last with Social Security?
faqs.answer: Social Security extends your timeline by covering part of your living costs and lowering the monthly draw taken from savings. If your household spends $10,000 a month and receives outside benefits, your portfolio withdrawal drops toward $6,000 or $8,000, extending a 20-year portfolio to 27 or 40 years.
